procedural_history.impugned_order: The Magistrate acquitted the accused (appellants) of charges under sections 420, 468, 406, and 465/471 of the Indian Penal Code and rejected the complainant's request to frame a charge under section 467 of the Indian Penal Code and commit the accused to the Court of Sessions.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The complainant appealed to the Patna High Court against the acquittal. The High Court, in Criminal Appeal No. 66 of 1962, held that the evidence prima facie disclosed an offense under section 467 of the Indian Penal Code. It set aside the acquittal and ordered a retrial, directing the Magistrate to frame a charge under section 467 and commit the accused to the Court of Session.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgment and order of the Patna High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on May 7, 1965, and provided their reasons later, affirming the High Court's jurisdiction to set aside the acquittal and order a retrial.

directions: Retrial ordered before the Court of Session.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the jurisdiction to set aside an acquittal and order a retrial when the trial Magistrate, despite having jurisdiction over the charges framed, ignored evidence of a more serious offence exclusively triable by a higher court.

facts: A trial Magistrate acquitted the accused of several charges over which he had jurisdiction.
During the trial, the Magistrate ignored evidence that prima facie disclosed a more serious offense (under s. 467, Indian Penal Code).
This more serious offense was exclusively triable by a higher court, the Court of Session.
The complainant appealed the acquittal to the High Court.
The High Court set aside the acquittal and ordered a retrial, holding that the Magistrate had a duty to frame the more serious charge and commit the case to the Court of Session.
law: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (ss. 417, 423), the High Court has the jurisdiction to set aside an order of acquittal and order a retrial.
This power should be exercised when the "justice of the case clearly demands it."
A Magistrate has a duty to apply the correct law and frame charges for all offenses prima facie disclosed by the evidence.
If the evidence discloses an offense exclusively triable by a higher court, the Magistrate cannot assume jurisdiction over the case by simply omitting that charge and trying only the lesser offenses.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument that the High Court had no jurisdiction because the Magistrate's trial was technically for offenses within his jurisdiction.
The Court reasoned that if this argument were accepted, there would be no remedy whenever a Magistrate improperly drops serious charges to retain a case they should have committed to a higher court.

The Court affirmed that a situation where a serious offense is omitted from the charge, especially when that offense would have ousted the trial court's jurisdiction, is a clear circumstance where the High Court can properly exercise its power to order a retrial.

The High Court was correct in finding that the Magistrate's failure to frame the charge for the more serious offense (s. 467) and commit the case to the Court of Session was an error that warranted intervention.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court acted within its jurisdiction. It confirmed that a High Court has the power to set aside an acquittal and order a retrial when a trial court improperly assumes jurisdiction by ignoring prima facie evidence of a more serious offense that is exclusively triable by a higher court.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate acts properly by trying an accused only for offences within his jurisdiction and ignoring a prima facie case for a more serious offence that would require committal to the Court of Session.

facts: A complaint was filed against the accused for several offences, including forgery.
The evidence presented to the Magistrate indicated a prima facie case for a serious offence under Section 467 of the Indian Penal Code, which is exclusively triable by the Court of Session.
Despite the complainant's request, the Magistrate declined to frame a charge under s. 467. Instead, he framed charges only for lesser offences over which he had jurisdiction.
The Magistrate proceeded with the trial on the lesser charges and ultimately acquitted the accused.

The complainant appealed to the High Court, which set aside the acquittal and ordered a retrial, holding that the Magistrate had a duty to frame the more serious charge and commit the case to the Court of Session.
law: A Magistrate has a duty to apply the correct law to the facts presented in a case.

If the evidence prima facie discloses an offence that is exclusively triable by a higher court (the Court of Session), the Magistrate must frame a charge for that offence and commit the case to that court.
It is improper for a Magistrate to selectively try only the offences that fall within his jurisdiction while ignoring evidence of a more serious offence that would oust his jurisdiction.

The High Court has the power, in an appeal against acquittal, to order a retrial if the interests of justice demand it. This power can be exercised when a serious offence, prima facie disclosed by evidence, was omitted from the charge, particularly when that offence would have removed the case from the trial court's jurisdiction.
application: The Supreme Court found that if the Magistrate had properly applied his mind to the evidence, he would have seen that a prima facie case for the main offence of forgery under s. 467 was made out, and the other offences were subsidiary.
The Court held that the Magistrate's duty was to frame the charge under s. 467 and commit the accused to the Court of Session. By choosing to try only the lesser offences, he acted improperly.
The Court rejected the argument that the High Court lacked jurisdiction to order a retrial because the Magistrate's trial was technically 'with jurisdiction' for the charges he chose to frame.
It reasoned that accepting such an argument would leave no remedy in situations where a Magistrate deliberately drops serious charges to improperly retain jurisdiction over a case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a Magistrate acts improperly by ignoring a prima facie case for a serious offence triable by a higher court and instead trying the accused only for lesser offences within his own jurisdiction. The Magistrate's clear duty is to frame the more serious charge and commit the case to the appropriate court for trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the jurisdiction to set aside an acquittal and order a retrial when the trial Magistrate, despite having jurisdiction over the charges framed, ignored evidence of a more serious offence exclusively triable by a higher court.
appellant_arguments: The trial before the Magistrate was conducted with jurisdiction and cannot be set aside merely because the High Court believed a more serious charge under s. 467 might be framed.
Ordering a retrial on such grounds is not a proceeding contemplated by s. 423(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
respondent_arguments: The trial before the Magistrate was without jurisdiction because the facts disclosed an offence under s. 467, which is exclusively triable by the Court of Session.
The Magistrate should have acted under Chapter XVIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure with a view to committing the accused to the Court of Session for trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate acts properly by trying an accused only for offences within his jurisdiction and ignoring a prima facie case for a more serious offence that would require committal to the Court of Session.
appellant_arguments: The Magistrate acted within his jurisdiction by trying the accused only for the offences for which charges were framed, over which he had authority.
respondent_arguments: It is the duty of the Magistrate to apply the correct law and frame charges for all offences disclosed by the facts, even if a more serious offence is exclusively triable by the Court of Session.
A Magistrate should not assume jurisdiction over a case by omitting a more serious charge that is prima facie made out by the evidence.

cases.case_name: Dr. Sanmukh Singh Teja Singh Yogi v. Emperor
cases.principle: It is a correct precedent for the High Court to set aside an acquittal and order a retrial where a Magistrate omits to frame a charge for a serious offence that is prima facie disclosed by the evidence, especially when that charge would have ousted the Magistrate's own jurisdiction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court, while hearing an appeal against an acquittal, has the jurisdiction to set aside the acquittal and order a retrial if the justice of the case demands it. This power is properly exercised when the trial court omitted a serious charge that was prima facie disclosed by evidence, particularly when that omitted charge, if framed, would have ousted the trial court's own jurisdiction. The fact that the trial court had jurisdiction over the lesser charges it did try does not negate the High Court's power to intervene.
obiter: However hesitant the High Court may be to set aside an order of acquittal and to order retrial, it has jurisdiction under the Code to do so.
If it were so there would be no remedy whenever a Magistrate dropped serious charges ousting him of his jurisdiction and tried only those within his jurisdiction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A Magistrate cannot properly assume jurisdiction over a case by choosing to try only those offences within his jurisdiction while ignoring a prima facie case for a more serious offence that is exclusively triable by a higher court. In such a situation, the Magistrate's duty is to frame the more serious charge and commit the accused for trial before the appropriate court, and the High Court has the jurisdiction to set aside an acquittal resulting from this error and order a retrial before the proper court.
legal_tests_applied: The High Court has jurisdiction under the Code of Criminal Procedure to set aside an acquittal and order a retrial if the justice of the case clearly demands it.

A case involving the omission from the charge of a serious offence prima facie disclosed by the evidence is a circumstance in which the power to order a retrial can properly be exercised, particularly when the charge for the omitted offence, if framed, would have ousted the trial court of its jurisdiction.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the High Court lacked jurisdiction because the Magistrate's trial was technically conducted with jurisdiction over the charges framed is incorrect. Accepting this argument would create a situation with no remedy when a Magistrate improperly drops serious charges to retain jurisdiction.

The contention that ordering a retrial robs the accused of the 'reinforcement of the presumption of innocence' is not persuasive, as the phrase is hardly apt to describe a case where the accused is acquitted without proper jurisdiction over the most serious prima facie offence.
why_respondent_won: The High Court correctly held that it was the duty of the Magistrate to apply the correct law; if the facts disclosed an offence exclusively triable by the Court of Session, he ought to have framed that charge and not assumed jurisdiction over the case by omitting it.

The evidence established a prima facie case for an offence under s. 467, Indian Penal Code, which is exclusively triable by the Court of Session. Therefore, the Magistrate's duty was to frame a charge under s. 467 and commit the appellants to stand trial before the Court of Session.

The High Court acted within its jurisdiction when it set aside the acquittal and ordered a retrial, as the omission of the serious charge which ousted the Magistrate's jurisdiction was a clear circumstance demanding such an intervention for the sake of justice.
policy_considerations: If the High Court could not set aside an acquittal in such circumstances, 'there would be no remedy whenever a Magistrate dropped serious charges ousting him of his jurisdiction and tried only those within his jurisdiction.'
While the power to set aside an acquittal and order a retrial must be used with great care and caution, it exists under the Code to be exercised when 'the justice of the case clearly demands it.'
